newsitem.title: FINLAND: Diabetes consequence of 'paradise lost', experts say.
newsitem.headline: Diabetes consequence of 'paradise lost', experts say.

text.p: While improved medical care, access to antibiotics and eradication of food scarcities in newly industrialising countries mean fewer infant deaths and stronger children, there is a deadly trade-off, diabetes experts said on Monday.
People who once battled infection and famine are now being picked off by so-called diseases of affluence, such as diabetes, heart disease and cancer.

People in developing countries, and those in less-advanced minorities in developed countries, should be encouraged to preserve many aspects of their "simpler" lifestyle, speakers at the 16th International Diabetes Federation Congress said.
The International Diabetes Federation predicts the rate of diabetes will rise by 45 percent in developed countries, but by 200 percent -- a tripling of the present rate -- in developing countries.

The World Health Organisation predicts nearly 300 million people will suffer from diabetes worldwide by 2025. Already diabetes and its associated problems may account for five to 10 percent of the health budgets of most countries, it says.

"Non-insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus (NIDDM) and obesity have reached alarming, and indeed epidemic, proportions not only in Polynesians, Micronesians, Melanesians, and migrant Asian Indians of the Pacific, but also in many other developing and newly industrialised populations in Asia, Africa and Latin America," said Paul Zimmet of the International Diabetes Institute.

Zimmet's team at Australia's Monash University has found that, among adults in the Pacific island state of Nauru, up to 35 percent have diabetes. Urban Samoans have a 12 percent rate compared to four percent of Australians of European descent.
Diabetes can cause heart disease, kidney failure and blindness. Damage that accumulates over the years by high blood sugar levels damages tiny blood vessels, leading to tissue death and gangrene.
It often goes hand-in-hand with obesity -- another high risk factor for heart disease and early death.
Like many other diseases that afflict modern people, diabetes is often the result of primitive bodies living in an increasingly wealthy world.

Jak Jervell, a Norwegian expert on diabetes who heads the International Diabetes Federation, noted emerging scientific evidence that diabetes is especially common in quickly developing societies, when babies are malnourished in the womb and as infants, but later get a rich diet.
People evolved in the days when food was scarce, they had to work hard for it, and what was there was not especially nutritious. People had to eat a lot to get by.
"Animals were difficult to catch and there is little fat on wild animals," Jervell said. People ate a lot of wild greens and other bulky, fibre-rich plant food.
"It was seldom possible to eat as much as you wanted and when you did, you enjoyed it," he added. Therefore, humans who liked to gorge themselves had a genetic advantage.
Getting food took a lot of energy, so people rested whenever they could. Lying around, watching television and eating high-fat and sugary snacks is only natural behaviour, he said.
"We are fighting against two to three million years of evolution of our species," Jervell said.
Zimmet said disease patterns showed that when people were quickly forced from a simple to a modern pattern of life, they developed diabetes.
"Yes, we have a major problem now," Zimmet said. "It cannot be treated by traditional medical methods."
Diet and exercise can control NIDDM, while insulin helps control the type-one or insulin-dependent variety. But going to the doctor for advice will not help people in developing societies.
"I don't think bringing in more drugs is going to help," Zimmet said.
"As long as people retain a traditional lifestyle of diet, plenty of exercise, living in the natural environment...they don't develop diabetes," he added.
